messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 40

He is 60 now, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his life on the water. He still calls himself a fisherman before anything else. Even on mornings when he does not go out, he wakes before dawn, sits on the edge of the bed, and listens for the wind as if his body has not learned there is sometimes nowhere it needs to be. He lives with his wife in the same coastal village where they raised their children. When he begins to speak about what brought him in, he does not start with himself. He starts with his younger brother.

Several years ago, during storm season, his brother joined him for a day’s fishing. They had worked together since they were boys, moving around each other on the boat with the kind of ease that comes from a lifetime of shared routines. That morning the sea was unsettled, but not unusual by their standards. He remembers telling his brother they would be quick. He remembers his brother laughing and saying they had gone out in worse.

What happened next still comes to him in fragments that feel sharper than ordinary memory. A wave struck at an angle he had not expected. The boat lurched hard. Nets shifted. His brother lost his footing and went over the side. He can still see one arm rise out of the water. He shouts this part when he tells it, as though his voice might still carry backward in time. He threw a line, then another. He turned the engine. Everything after that feels both too fast and endless. The water was rough, brown-green, churning around the hull. He remembers his own hands slipping, the taste of salt, the sound of the motor fighting the current. He did not get to him in time.

He is the one who came back to shore. He is the one who had to tell the family.

In the first months afterward, he does not sleep much. When he closes his eyes, he sees his brother’s hand disappearing under the surface. Sometimes the image arrives before he is fully asleep, and he jerks upright, breathing hard, already wet with sweat. His wife tells him he cries out at night. He does not remember the words, only the panic in his chest and the certainty, for a few seconds after waking, that he is still on the boat and must move quickly or someone will die.

He returns to fishing because he does not know how not to. The sea is his livelihood, and staying home makes him feel useless and ashamed. But the work changes. He checks the ropes over and over. He studies the sky with a vigilance that leaves him exhausted before the day has properly begun. If another man on the boat stands too close to the edge, his whole body tightens. He snaps at younger fishermen for taking risks he once considered normal. Loud slaps of water against the hull make him flinch. On bad days he turns back early, telling others the catch is poor or the engine sounds wrong, unable to admit that his hands are trembling.

He avoids the stretch of shore where families gather after a boat returns. For a long time, he cannot look at his brother’s widow without feeling a crushing weight in his chest. At home he becomes quieter, then irritable. His wife says he is present in body but not in spirit. Small things provoke him: a dropped plate, children shouting in the lane, the television playing storm footage. He hates the anger because it does not fit the man he believes himself to be, but it comes quickly, before thought. Then he withdraws, sitting outside alone, smoking and staring toward the water.

He carries guilt with a kind of stubborn devotion. He tells himself he should have read the weather differently, should have insisted they stay in port, should have moved faster, thrown better, done something more. When others remind him the sea can take even the most careful men, he nods without accepting it. In his mind, his brother died in front of him, and that fact has arranged itself into a private verdict.

Now, years later, his life is narrower than it once was. He still works, though less often in rough weather and rarely with company he does not trust. He sits with his back to walls in tea shops. He scans faces in crowds. During heavy rain, his heart starts pounding before he is aware of any thought. Some evenings his grandson climbs into his lap, and for a few minutes he softens, telling stories about fish, tides, and moonlight on the water. Then a sudden splash from the nearby canal or the low growl of distant thunder pulls his eyes away. His wife notices how quickly he goes elsewhere, how the room leaves him even when he has not stood up.

He says he wants peace. What he means is that he wants one day in which the sea is only the sea again, and not the place where he lost his brother while trying, and failing, to bring him home.
